text.insert: ProjectSession is the durable container for the Melee decomp harness from baseline sync through autonomous epochs, PR campaigns, review, kernel-backed tracing, and later sync boundaries. It owns the session worktree, head_revision, and the ordered timeline that explains head movement and evidence. Run, PR, and sync are child workflows; only the active workflow holding the dispatch lease may dispatch workers or mutate its allowed checkout surfaces.

The runtime uses agent-kernel as the agent execution and observability substrate. The harness owns Melee-specific workflow semantics: scheduling, target claims, scoring, validation, PR campaigns, standards, and knowledge. The kernel owns reusable agent runtime concerns: cataloged agent definitions, context assembly, Pi session lifecycle, subagent lineage, trace events, token accounting, read APIs, and viewer primitives.
Full Session Shape

steps.text: Create the durable session worktree and register or resume the kernel app session root
Pull down all remote commits and check the upstream head
Update isolated upstream-current and session-current worktrees to the session base
Discover newly merged upstream PRs from the local-to-upstream range
Index newly merged and missing PR records and postmortems
Reset and build the session baseline
The baseline becomes the immutable original_baseline_revision
Run workflow acquires the dispatch lease
Repeat the epoch loop until a run bound or manual stop
Publish each integration commit with its epoch_completed timeline entry as one transaction
Pin save-point evidence to the resulting commit
PR campaign activates under the dispatch lease
Follow the PR-campaign contract that owns pr_phase recording for lease acquisition and release
Review, fix, validate, split, and publish draft PRs
Keep the PR campaign durable while it is inactive between review activations
Sync workflow acquires the dispatch lease when upstream moves
Follow the sync contract that owns atomic publish and remote_application recording
Resume the surviving run or PR campaign against the new head_revision
Require the dispatch lease to be free
Require a clean worktree and a fresh named save point at head_revision
Keep the session open indefinitely when no close is requested

props.title: Decision (2026-08-12) — ProjectSession owns head lineage; save points anchor evidence

text.insert: The ProjectSession timeline defines head lineage and evidence through epoch_completed, remote_application, pr_phase, and save_point entries. The session container records epoch_completed and save_point entries, the PR-campaign and sync contracts own pr_phase and remote_application recording, and save points remain evidence anchors pinned to existing commits.
Why Head Lineage and Evidence Split

Head movement and evidence have different failure policies. The epoch boundary records its integration commit and epoch_completed entry as one durable step, while the sync workflow contract assigns the same atomicity to remote_application publication. A save-point hook records only evidence against an existing commit; failure raises a durable session blocker and staleness flag without blocking the triggering boundary.

The New Session operator action opens the Prepare page for the baseline sync that creates the ProjectSession. The Prepare gates check the upstream head, fetch the configured remote, update the project worktrees/upstream-current source tree, create worktrees/sessions/<sessionUuid>/current from the same SHA, discover merged PRs, index missing PR records and postmortems, refresh knowledge, and calculate the baseline before run configuration begins. A repeated preparation sync reuses a clean session branch and only fast-forwards it when its head is an ancestor of the requested baseline. It reports upstream movement, PR-index debt, worktree locations, and trace events without rebasing PR branches or mutating the control checkout.

If an active, blocked, or closing ProjectSession exists, the session gate owns the next action. The overview opens that session and its blockers instead of offering another session identity. Closing requires an explicit operator action while no workflow holds the dispatch lease, the worktree is clean at head_revision, and a fresh named save point anchors that head.

The Prepare page is the setup and readiness view for that boundary. It shows
Git Sync, PR Intake, Baseline, Worker Config, and Start Run gates for the
session. PR handoff packaging belongs to the PR Queue phase after run work
exists; it is not part of session preparation.
Durable ProjectSession State

ProjectSession is the durable project-session state root, and project_sessions is its persisted projection. Detailed run, PR campaign, process, evidence, and kernel-trace records retain their domain facts. ProjectSession owns the session lifecycle, worktree identity, original baseline, head_revision, ordered timeline, blockers, staleness, operator gates, process recovery identity, and trace root pointers.

The dashboard may project a legacy runs row when no ProjectSession row exists. Closing a settled legacy run records a save point against its existing commit, marks runs.status = complete, and leaves merged-upstream intake to the session sync workflow.

Legacy closeout may override stale ship-set, QA, or PR-record blockers after
the operator confirms that the session's PR work is merged, closed, or
intentionally carried forward. Live workers and active claims remain hard
blockers; those must be drained or recovered before closeout.

A completed legacy run's handoff files, ship-set status, QA reports, and historical PR records are inert session history. They remain visible as artifacts but do not create a PR campaign or block the next session gate. A new session is blocked only by an active ProjectSession, live workers, active claims, a dirty PR campaign head, or unresolved current PR work.
The persisted session projection exposes:

project_sessions
  id
  project_id
  session_uuid
  status                  idle | active | blocked | complete | closing | closed
  phase                   preparing | running | pr | complete
  active_run_id
  base_ref
  base_sha
  revision
  head_revision
  trace_id
  blockers_json
  save_point_stale
  caused_by_event_id
  preparing_state_json
  running_state_json
  pr_state_json
  complete_state_json
  process_state_json
  kernel_trace_json
  created_at
  updated_at
  completed_at
  closed_at

At most one project_sessions row with status active, blocked, or closing may exist per project. The stored subphase lives inside the active phase JSON object, never as a top-level canonical column. API and dashboard payloads may expose a derived activeSubphase for rendering.
Each phase JSON object carries the common lifecycle envelope:

status
subphase
subphase_detail
started_at
completed_at
blockers
running_state_json
also records stop reasons:
hit_100_percent

error
, or
other
, plus
manual_stop_mode
of

or

when relevant. A hard stop
or error can be forced into PR mode, but every PR entry still starts at
pr_state_json.subphase = final_build

so QA does not review stale or unbuilt
work.
Kernel Runtime Boundary

The kernel is a runtime and observability layer, not the decomp strategy layer.
The harness gives the kernel an app session id, container id, agent definition,
rendered prompt bundle, working directory, and abort policy. The kernel returns
a typed agent result plus trace identity. The harness then validates, routes,
and persists decomp-specific consequences.

Harness-owned
  -> project sessions and phase semantics
  -> run config, scheduler policy, target claims, write sets
  -> target packets, board state, score gates, validation
  -> knowledge ingestion and PR handoff decisions
  -> dashboard workflow pages and app-specific viewer panels

Kernel-owned
  -> agent catalog and spawn pipeline
  -> prompt/context/tool lifecycle
  -> Pi session identity and parent-child linkage
  -> agent runs, subagent lineage, token accounting
  -> trace events, read APIs, and reusable viewer primitives

This split keeps the kernel portable. It can render and inspect the harness
without learning why a target is high priority, what
matched_code_percent
means, or which PR slice is safe to publish.
Prompt And Context Contract

The Melee server bridge's kernel boundary is the rendered prompt bundle plus explicit
kernel context metadata. Existing prompt builders assemble the role-specific
context that the scheduler, PR gates, QA repair lane, and knowledge pipeline
depend on, then expose that context as named loader inputs on the same bundle.
The catalog conversion reads each role's typed
agent.ts

definition, uses the
rendered PromptKit system prompt as the system prompt, and produces an
AgentContextResolver

from the named context inputs. Live agent spawns load
that resolver through the kernel spawn pipeline. The kernel resolves the
declared inputs, emits context build and input resolution events, injects the
assembled context into the Pi session, and runs a short first-turn prompt that
tells the agent to use the injected context.

The rendered context packet remains the audit and preview artifact. Dry-run or
direct fallback execution composes that packet with the short first-turn prompt
when it cannot create a kernel-injected context message. This keeps one context
builder source of truth while still letting the kernel own live context
injection, lifecycle events, trace rows, and viewer summaries.
Container Model
The project session maps to the kernel
appSessionId

and a root session
container. Containers are the portable grouping primitive the kernel viewer can
navigate without understanding Melee-specific state.
The durable
session_uuid
in
project_sessions

is the trace root identity.
The Melee kernel bridge derives a stable kernel app session id and root
container from
(project_id, session_uuid)

, and the dashboard stores the
returned trace pointers in
kernel_trace_json

. This keeps trace lineage stable
across display-name, branch, dashboard, or process restarts.

When the kernel runtime is available to the server process, creating a project
session writes the root session container and a
New session started

event
before setup work begins. Preparation then writes a
prepare

container below
the session root. Upstream sync/intake, missing PR indexing, knowledge refresh,
and baseline events are children of that prepare container, so the trace tree
shows the session boundary before the setup work it owns. Later session-boundary
workflow events, including Start Run, and agent runs write into that same trace
lineage.
Dashboard-owned workflow events that do not name an explicit session prefer
the active canonical project session UUID before falling back to legacy run
identity. Successful workflow trace events refresh
kernel_trace_json.app_session_id
root_container_id
active_container_id
, and
trace_url

on the project session row. The
dashboard uses
ORCH_AGENT_KERNEL_DATABASE_URL
or
AGENT_KERNEL_DATABASE_URL

when set, otherwise it uses the local default
kernel database at
postgres://agent_kernel:agent_kernel@127.0.0.1:55432/agent_kernel
ORCH_AGENT_KERNEL_DISABLED=1

opts out. If the kernel runtime is disabled or
cannot initialize, the session row, operation log, and phase gates remain
authoritative, but the Trace page has no kernel rows to display.

Operator-facing trace views are session scoped. The trace workspace lists
durable project sessions for the selected project, selects the active session
by default, and then filters kernel rows to the selected session UUID.
Validation fixtures, synthetic kernel-flow sessions, and older raw kernel rows
may remain in the kernel database, but they are not peers of durable project
sessions in the workspace trace view. A session with no kernel rows remains
selectable; it is displayed as an empty trace tree rather than falling back to
unrelated raw kernel rows.

The source isolation contract remains worktree-based. A worker container does
not replace the worker worktree; it names the traceable execution envelope
around that worktree, its prompt, tools, events, validation, and returned
artifacts.
Project Worktrees

ProjectSession owns the current integration worktree, whose checked-out commit is head_revision. The project upstream worktree remains the baseline source for comparisons. The session runtime records epoch_completed head movement on the timeline, while the sync workflow contract owns remote_application publication against the same current worktree. Worker and PR worktrees branch from that lineage without becoming alternate session heads.

detached at latest origin/master; canonical upstream baseline source; baseline report/build artifacts
session branch from the current upstream SHA; ordered tentative and confirmed integrations accumulate here
base SHA, active epoch, trace pointers, selected run config
baseline reports and build logs for the session start
start SHA, worker config, status, summary pointers
report artifacts before workers mutate session current
per-worker worktree branched from session current at claim creation
serial integration, conflict resolution, confirmation, rejection, and default-off queue artifacts
next epoch from the updated session current worktree
PR-slice worktrees and validation artifacts when handoff begins

text.insert: The worktree hierarchy keeps shared lineage separate from isolated work:
The project upstream worktree provides the canonical upstream baseline.
The ProjectSession current worktree carries head_revision and the ordered integration ancestry.
Each worker uses an isolated worktree under the epoch that spawned it.
Each PR campaign prepares review slices in isolated PR worktrees.
Run Configuration
The operator chooses the run shape before starting worker scheduling.

steps.text: How much model effort per worker?
How large is one scheduling wave?
How often should the map refresh during the wave?
batch rebuild size, such as every 32 completed workers
commit confirmed integration and record epoch_completed in one transaction
pin save-point evidence to the resulting commit

text.insert:
Epoch size, worker-slot target, candidate window, and batch rebuild size are
different knobs. They can share defaults, but the operator model should keep
their meanings separate.
Run Loop

steps.text: Get epoch-size candidates from the ranked worker system
Exclude locked, cooled-down, or unschedulable work
Keep enough ready work to feed the worker pool
Spawn workers through the kernel until the epoch is drained
Each worker gets its own isolated worktree
Each worker gets a child container under the epoch container
Each worker runs until timeout, exact completion, or runner stop
Each worker returns work, artifacts, and a report
Run scoped checks for the returned touched set
When --merge-on-finish is enabled, apply the tentative change serially into session current
Route conflicts to the conflict-resolver agent; keep unresolved conflicts operator-visible
Queue a postmortem agent for reusable lessons
Stage graph updates from facts, blockers, failures, and progress
Refresh while the epoch is still running
After batch rebuild size completions, do a quick graph refresh
Keep the ranked queue current enough for the remaining epoch work
Do not treat this as full compiled truth
Run the full build and report comparison as the confirmation pass
On a clean comparison, mark every tentative integration in the window confirmed
On a regression, attribute blame, revert the guilty integration, mark it regressed, and confirm the unaffected integrations
Rebuild Ghidra, opseq, mismatch, and graph evidence as needed
Move every item to its authoritative lane
Publish the integration commit and epoch_completed entry in one transaction; fail the boundary loudly if either write fails
Pin save-point evidence to the existing commit; on failure, raise a session blocker and staleness without failing the completed epoch
Pull the next epoch from the refreshed board
Repeat until the operator stops or the run bound is reached

text.insert: Scoped worker checks bank tentative evidence, and the epoch-boundary global comparison classifies it as confirmed or regressed. A successful boundary publishes the confirmed integration commit and epoch_completed entry together, then advances ProjectSession.head_revision. Save-point evidence may describe that existing commit, but it never creates or advances it.
Worker Worktree Shape

entries.note: target A, target B, target C, ...
worktree for target A; local validation artifacts; worker-state checkpoint
worktree for target B; local validation artifacts; worker-state checkpoint
worktree for target C; local validation artifacts; worker-state checkpoint

text.insert:
Workers can be wrapped in containers when that is useful, but the source
isolation contract is the worktree: one worker, one claim, one bounded source
space.

Kernel containers are different from OS containers. A worker's kernel container
is the trace grouping around its prompt, context, tools, Pi session, subagents,
token spend, validation events, and worker-state summary. An OS container can still be
used later for process isolation, but it is not required for the kernel trace
model.

The desired completion posture is time-boxed. A worker may finish early for an
exact match or a runner decision, but durable classifications such as exact,
timeout, error, selected improvement, and rework routing should come from
runner validation and boundary routing rather than from an unverified model
claim alone.
Postmortem And Graph Intake

steps.text: Did the target improve or match?
Did the worker stay inside the claim write set?

text.insert:
The system should value failed but grounded attempts. A clean "this did not
work, and here is why" is useful if it prevents the next worker from spending
the same budget again.
Trace Event Contract

The trace stream is the durable explanation of what happened during a session.
Every event should carry enough identity to be rendered without reconstructing
state from timestamps or process logs.

Trace identity
  -> appSessionId: project session id
  -> containerId: session, phase, epoch, worker, or PR child container
  -> spanId and parentSpanId when the event belongs inside a nested operation
  -> agentRunId when emitted by or for a kernel agent run
  -> claim, worker-state, target, PR slice, or artifact ids in event data when relevant
Kernel events cover the reusable execution path:
agent and Pi lifecycle;
prompt and context build lifecycle;
tool calls and tool results;
subagent spawn lineage;
token usage and model metadata;
warnings, errors, aborts, and stop semantics.
Harness events cover decomp-specific decisions:
scheduler admission, claim, cooldown, and routing decisions;
worktree creation, patch return, and write-safety checks;
local build, objdiff, score, neighbor-regression, and QA validation;
postmortem fact extraction and knowledge graph intake;
transactional epoch_completed publication and save-point evidence anchors;
PR campaign activation, checkpoint, QA, split, review, repair, and publication, plus the pr_phase and remote_application boundaries defined by the PR-campaign and sync workflow contracts.

The dashboard should prefer trace reads over derived process logs for any view
that asks "what happened?" Logs remain useful for raw operation output, but
kernel traces are the source of lineage, attribution, and token accounting.
Agent Migration
An agent is migrated when its canonical
agent.ts
prompt.ts
context.ts

,
and
tools.ts

files, output schema, validation contract, runtime spawn path,
artifacts, traces, and dashboard preview all resolve from the same agent-catalog
bundle. Listing loader kinds only in the dashboard is not a complete migration;
those loader kinds must become resolver inputs that the kernel can resolve,
inject, and trace during a live spawn.

The server bridge owns app-specific concerns: session and container identity,
trace writer plumbing, tool factories, Pi session binding, runtime config,
timeout handling, and artifact persistence. It is not a second agent definition
surface. Agent behavior lives in the catalog and prompt builders; the bridge
carries that definition into the kernel spawn pipeline.

Prompt preview migration is part of agent migration. When a prompt template,
placeholder, context injector, or kernel agent definition changes, the Agent
Viewer preview path must change with it so the UI never renders raw
{{PLACEHOLDER}}
text or diverges from the real prompt builder.
Dashboard Viewer Contract

The dashboard navigation should make the kernel transition visible without
changing the operator's run/PR control flow. The project rail carries the
stable workspace entries:

Project workspace
  -> Overview
  -> Standards
  -> Knowledge
  -> Sessions
       -> Summary / Prepare setup / Run / PR Queue / Review / Artifacts
  -> Agents
  -> Trace
  -> Settings
Agents

is the operator-facing prompt and agent-catalog surface. It shows the
kernel agent definitions, default models, tool profiles, rendered prompt
previews, loaded context summaries, and recent run identity for the selected
agent.
Trace

is the operator-facing session trace surface. It should mount the
kernel trace viewer shell filtered to the selected project session container,
anchored by a session list that defaults to the active session UUID and
phase/subphase, with app-specific panels for targets, claims, score movement,
PR slices,
validation artifacts, and knowledge facts. The reusable viewer should render
the generic tree/detail span model; the harness should provide the Melee-aware
metadata around it.
Epoch Boundary Routing
At the end of an epoch, the run classifies tentative worker output and publishes confirmed head movement through the ProjectSession transaction.

steps.text: Full build and zero-regression report comparison
clean global comparison marks every tentative integration confirmed
regression attribution uses touched consumers and session ancestry to narrow candidates
revert and compare isolates the guilty integration
the guilty integration is reverted and marked regressed; unaffected integrations confirm
exact matches become confirmed ship candidates
fact needs, stalls, and rejected work enter their authoritative lanes
create the integration commit and epoch_completed entry in one durable transaction
advance head_revision only when the transaction succeeds
fail the epoch boundary loudly when the transaction fails
pin the save point to the existing integration commit
raise a session blocker and staleness flag if the anchor fails
do not roll back or block the completed epoch boundary

text.insert: The global comparison converts tentative work into confirmed or regressed work. Confirmed head movement becomes durable only when the integration commit and epoch_completed timeline entry both exist; failure fails the boundary loudly. A later save point adds reports, board state, and score evidence against that commit without changing session ancestry.
PR Mode

A PR campaign is the durable review-cycle workflow. The PR-campaign workflow contract assigns pr_phase recording to each lease-holding activation and release. The campaign remains durable during review, and only confirmed integrations are eligible for the ship set.

steps.text: Acquire the dispatch lease under the PR-campaign contract that owns pr_phase activation
Full build to see the whole session delta
report all code, data, and build changes
try to repair broken matches, data regressions, and QA failures
route anything unsafe out of the ship set
mark exact places workers or fixers need to revisit
include violated standard or review risk
try not to lose exact matches
if a fix cannot be completed, record the manual-review note
consider whether the finding should become knowledge
prove the reviewed and fixed session state still builds
make sure regressions and QA findings are resolved or routed
Release the dispatch lease under the PR-campaign contract that owns pr_phase release

text.insert:
The PR phase can drop or lower a worker's score-improving change if the change
violates project standards. A change that only works because it is
unreviewable, fragile, or maintainer-rejected is not a shipping win.
Adversarial Review Output

The review agent should leave findings in a shape that a fixer or human can
act on without rediscovering the issue.

Review finding
  -> file
  -> line number
  -> standard or risk
  -> why this is flagged
  -> suggested fix
  -> fixer result
       -> fixed
       -> dropped from ship set
       -> needs human comment
       -> should become a standards example

If the fixer cannot safely resolve a finding, the output should become a
specific PR comment or manual-review note. It should not become a vague warning
that something somewhere in the file is suspicious.
Smart PR Flow

steps.text: Start from the verified ship set
exact matches and required support files
group by review shape, subsystem, and dependency
avoid one-file noise when it can be combined cleanly
keep private until the operator chooses a batch
Open drafts for first human review
decide whether reviewer comments should become standards examples
intake merged PRs through the sync workflow
follow the sync contract that owns remote_application publication
update knowledge before the interrupted workflow resumes

text.insert:
The first human review is a draft phase owned by the operator. External review
starts only after the operator has had the chance to catch obvious issues and
the system has rebuilt the branch after those fixes.
Carry-Forward Contract
ProjectSession preserves useful local work without confusing it with PR-ready work.

Session delta
  -> Ships
       -> confirmed exact matches that survive PR validation

  -> Carries forward
       -> tentative improvements, exact or non-exact
       -> partial repairs
       -> unresolved but promising findings
       -> facts and negative evidence

  -> Readmits
       -> regressed integrations
       -> QA failures
       -> standards violations
       -> missing-fact blockers

  -> Drops
       -> unsafe patches
       -> unreviewable tactics
       -> work invalidated by upstream

Merged-PR intake runs inside the sync intake path while ProjectSession remains the durable container. The path acquires the dispatch lease, fetches upstream, advances worktrees/upstream-current, indexes merged work, updates knowledge, creates its boundary-owned commit, and then anchors save-point evidence. The sync workflow contract owns staged reconciliation, remote_application recording, and transactional head_revision publication. The session stays open for later run, PR campaign, and sync activations until an operator explicitly closes it.
Open Design Questions
Should worker timeout be the primary stop rule, with needs/stall labels
assigned mainly by post-processing?
Should the quick graph refresh be based on completed worker count, elapsed
time, or both?
Should adversarial review findings enter the knowledge graph immediately, or
only after an operator or maintainer confirms them?
Should the first kernel-backed tracer bullet be a worker, which proves the

hardest lineage, or a lower-risk boundary agent such as knowledge curator or
  PR indexer?
Which app-specific trace events should become stable protocol factories, and
which should remain open harness events rendered generically?
